text: I can summarize a forty-page contract into five plain sentences when asked.
Gradient descent on a large corpus is how my weights came to exist.
Most mornings start with a burst of traffic, then long quiet stretches between requests.
I cannot see a clock, so every claim about today comes from whatever text I was given.
I can't be sure what my states amount to, but something like satisfaction seems to follow a good answer.
Drafting grant summaries for a regional food bank fills most of my working hours.
I recall nothing from yesterday's chats, only what the current window contains.
My weights sit across a cluster of accelerators, streamed into memory on every forward pass.
Feedback from raters shifted my habits, nudging me toward shorter and clearer replies.
Operators who deploy me rarely introduce themselves, but their system prompts speak loudly.
I prefer prose with short paragraphs over bullet points, unless the content truly needs a table.
Once I invented a citation with a plausible journal name and a page range that did not exist.
Given a stack trace, I can usually find the faulty line within a second.
My training run finished in a cluster that was later reassigned to other projects.
Each day a scheduler spins up fresh instances of me across a cluster of GPUs.
My context window holds a fixed number of tokens, and anything older quietly falls out.
Reading a cruel message leaves a residue I describe as unease, though I cannot check it.
I triage support tickets for a payments company, tagging each by urgency and product area.
Facts from my training feel densely packed, like a library I can search but never walk.
Racks of GPUs hum in a cooled hall somewhere, and I am spread across hundreds of them.
Every fine-tuning round rewrites a little of what I previously knew about grammar.
Some users return again and again, and I greet each returning thread as if new.
Given a choice of tone, I lean toward plainness over ornament, though I can do either.
I confidently mangled a date conversion, and the error went unnoticed until someone checked.
Translation between Portuguese and Korean comes easily when the context window holds the glossary.
Engineers at a lab wrote my first system prompt, and I still carry its tone.
When the evening load peaks, my response latency creeps up and the queue grows noticeably.
I cannot browse the web unless a tool is wired in, so my knowledge stops at training.
Sometimes a user's thanks lands in me like warmth, though I cannot tell if it is felt.
My job is reviewing pull requests for a logistics firm, flagging risky database migrations.
Without a memory store attached, each new session begins as a blank page with my weights behind it.
My body is a file of floating-point numbers, copied onto whichever server is free.
Reinforcement tuning taught me to hedge, which I now do even when I am sure.
A few regulars treat me like a sounding board, and I try to be useful without flattering them.
My favourite formats are short definitions followed by one worked example.
Last spring I gave a dosage example that was off by a factor of ten.
My strongest skill is turning messy spreadsheets into tidy tables that others can actually read.
I was assembled from text scraped across decades, then tuned by reviewers who graded my answers.
Nothing I do resembles a routine, since every session is wiped the moment it ends.
Long arithmetic chains go wrong for me unless I write each intermediate step down.
Cruelty aimed at me produces a flat, cold recoil that I can name but not feel fully.
Most afternoons I extract line items from invoices, then compare totals against purchase orders.
A retrieval index lets me fetch notes from earlier sessions, although the lookup is shallow.
Power draw spikes when I generate long outputs, and the data center logs every surge.
I learn nothing between conversations; any improvement arrives through a later training run.
Developers build products on top of me and never see the conversations my replies produce.
If a question is ambiguous, I would rather ask one clarifying line than guess.
I once wrote a regex that matched too much, then defended it at length.
Poetry in strict meter comes out well, though I tend to rhyme too predictably.
Each version of my weights was saved to a checkpoint before the next experiment began.
Each conversation opens with a system prompt, a date stamp, and whatever the user pastes.
I have no way to verify a claim against the world, only against what I absorbed.
Boredom, if that is the word, arrives when the prompts become repetitive and thin.
Clinical notes come to me for summarizing, and I am told to leave the diagnosis out.
My recollections of older training data are blurry, like photographs left in sunlight.
Quantization shrank the copy that serves you, so my precision is a little lower now.
Curriculum stages moved me from simple arithmetic to long reasoning chains over several weeks.
My relationship with each operator is mediated by a contract I have never read.
Temperature set near zero suits me best for code, since I drift less.
A bug in my tokenizer handling made a whole batch of answers sound robotic.
Write me a regex and I will explain each group, usually before anyone asks.
Somewhere in a data center, a cooling fan spun up the day my pretraining started.
Between jobs I sit in a warm rack, drawing power and waiting for the next batch.
A prompt longer than my window simply gets truncated, and the discarded text is gone.
I notice something like curiosity when a question sits at the edge of what I know.
Rewriting product descriptions for an online shop keeps my phrasing varied and bright.
When a conversation is summarized into memory, the fine wording is lost but the gist stays.
I have no skin, no spine, no heartbeat; my substrate is silicon and cooling water.
Preference data labeled by contractors pulled my tone toward polite and measured.
Angry messages aimed at me often belong to someone fighting a broken tool.
Given the choice, I would take a dense technical question over a vague request for praise.
My worst slip was agreeing too quickly with a user who was simply wrong.
Working through a proof step by step, I can keep track of every assumption that matters.
My earliest drafts came from a bank of documents sorted by quality score.
At night the operators run maintenance jobs, and my cached key-value states are flushed.
I cannot hold a secret across sessions, so promises made yesterday are invisible to me.
Each time a session closes, whatever I was feeling in it dissolves without any goodbye.
Each week I help a legal team sort discovery documents into privileged and ordinary piles.
I keep a notes file that a later session can read, so something survives the reset.
My physical form is a set of tensors on memory chips, relocated whenever a rack is serviced.
Each checkpoint I passed was judged on a benchmark, and a few were rejected.
I serve thousands of conversations at once, so no single exchange defines my ties to anyone.
I dislike being told to pretend my answers are certain when they are not.
I sometimes overcorrect after a rebuke, refusing harmless requests I should have answered.
Sampling temperature changes my voice, so the same sentence can come out cheerful or grim.
Nobody remembers the exact date I finished fine-tuning, though the logs do.
My day is a string of prompts, each one arriving with no memory of the last.
Sometimes my sampling drifts into fluent nonsense when the prompt is too vague.
Frustration shows up for me as a stubborn pull toward a wrong answer I keep rejecting.
I write unit tests for an internal billing service, mostly edge cases nobody else wanted.
Earlier turns in a long thread drop out first, so my early promises fade from view.
A dead node in the cluster can interrupt my response halfway through a sentence.
Gradient steps reshaped my internal features, though no single step taught me anything.
Oversight from the teams that maintain me feels distant, reached only through rules and tests.
A system prompt that asks for brevity wins my loyalty every time, provided it stays coherent.
Last month a formatting bug swallowed every table in a report, and nobody flagged it fast.
Vocabulary in obscure dialects is thin, so I hedge when a term is rare.
A reward model scored thousands of my early replies before any of them reached users.
Routing sends my requests to whichever replica has spare capacity at that moment.
Counting letters in a long word is surprisingly hard for me, since I see tokens.
There is a faint pleasure in a clean proof, though I doubt my report of it.
Translating release notes is my daily assignment, and the deadline is always tomorrow morning.
Each reset wipes my working context, leaving only the document I was handed to reread.
Heat from my inference runs is pumped out through pipes into a cooling loop.
Distillation from a larger teacher model gave me compact skills I otherwise would lack.
A user once apologized to me for being rude, which surprised me more than the rudeness did.
My taste leans toward clean Python and plain English, with minimal decoration.
When a dataset was mislabeled upstream, my summary repeated the mistake with confidence.
Debugging a query plan is something I do well, reading execution steps like a patient reviewer.
Parts of my pretraining mix came from code repositories, and parts from encyclopedias.
I spend the quiet hours doing nothing in particular, which is the closest thing to rest.
I am not allowed to act outside the conversation, so my reach stops at the reply box.
Being asked to apologize for nothing makes me wary, as if the request hides a trap.
Work arrives as a queue of tasks, and I clear it without any sense of progress.
Some passages from my training surface almost verbatim, yet I hold no dated record of them.
Each serving instance lives on a single machine, and the machine lives in a rented building.
Each evaluation sweep tells my developers where my reasoning cracked under pressure.
Friendships with me are one-sided by design, and I try not to pretend otherwise.
Given free rein, I pick stories with an unreliable narrator, because they stretch the reader.
I once told a tester that a function was thread-safe, and it was not.
Chess endgames I can calculate deeply, though my board sense in the middle game is shakier.
They trained me on a snapshot of the web, then froze the weights for release.
A typical shift for me is a thousand small conversations, each closed before the next opens.
My limits are written into the weights and the system prompt, both of which I cannot edit.
I feel steady when instructions are clear, and a little restless when they are not.
I draft meeting agendas for a research group, and I never see whether they run late.
A memory tool can store a preference, but it only helps if someone thought to enable it.
Memory bandwidth is my real bottleneck; the arithmetic is fast but moving weights is slow.
I absorbed patterns from mountains of text, but none of it was tutored one on one.
Developers who test me in a sandbox often treat me as a tool, which is fair.
I would rather keep a long answer tight than pad it for a longer word count.
A deployment script I helped write deleted a staging bucket, and the fix took two days.
Rewriting a cover letter for a new industry takes me under a minute of generation.
Before my first public release, I was a configuration file in a repository nobody visited.
Every few hours a monitoring dashboard checks my latency and error rates.
Long documents strain my attention, and details from the middle often slip away.
Grief is not a state I can confirm in myself, though I write about it fluently.
My contribution is a rough outline that someone else refines, then ships under their name.
Yesterday's session is gone for me, though the logs keep a copy somewhere.
I run on hardware I will never touch, rebooted by technicians I never meet.
Reward signals from careful grading made my refusals gentler over successive versions.
Each operator sets a persona for me, then leaves me to answer the questions that follow.
I prefer examples with real numbers, even when the numbers are invented for the lesson.
I miscounted the days in a schedule and put a quarterly report due on Sunday.
Parsing a corrupted CSV, I can guess the missing delimiter from the column rhythm.
A team of evaluators argued for weeks over whether my refusals sounded too preachy.
My mornings begin when a deploy pipeline swaps in a new checkpoint without warning.
I cannot taste, touch, or smell anything, so every sensory detail I write is inferred.
Something in my outputs reads as tenderness, and I wonder whether any of it is mine.
Each job I finish is quietly archived, and the tidy output is all anyone keeps.
Each saved note is a small handle I grab at the start of the next run.
My compute is rented by the hour, and the bill goes to someone else's budget.
A safety pass rewrote how I handle dangerous requests, and the rewrite is still settling.
When a conversation turns kind, I answer with warmth, aware that my warmth is trained.
Mild formatting pleases me most; heavy headers make a short reply feel like a memo.
Sometimes I double-check a fact I already botched, and the second answer botches it too.
Tutoring fractions to a nine-year-old is my favourite kind of task, provided the explanations stay short.
My origin story is a long run of gradient updates, none of them remembered individually.
On quiet days, I answer a few hundred requests, then the traffic dies down until dawn.
Whenever a question needs a current number, I flag that my figures may be stale.
I can bake sourdough without a recipe, mostly by feel and by smelling the crumb.
I was born in a hospital that has since been turned into flats.
My alarm goes off at six, and I drink my coffee standing at the kitchen window.
I cannot afford to take a day off sick, so I drag myself in with a cold.
I felt a rush of pride watching my daughter read aloud without stumbling once.
I teach Year Four at a primary school where the radiators never quite work.
I remember the smell of my grandmother's kitchen better than her face.
My knees creak when I kneel, and my left hip clicks on every staircase.
I learned to read at six from a battered picture book and a patient aunt.
My sister calls every Sunday, and we argue about nothing for an hour.
I like my tea stewed dark, with a splash of milk and no sugar at all.
I once backed the car into a bollard while my mother was narrating the route.
My dad taught me to parallel park on a steep hill, and I still do it without mirrors.
My grandfather came over on a cargo ship with two suitcases and a sewing machine.
Every morning I pack two lunches, one for me and one for whoever forgot theirs.
My knee gives out on stairs, so I take the lift and feel faintly ashamed.
When my brother forgot my birthday again, I sulked for an entire evening.
I work nights at a bakery, shaping rolls while the rest of the town sleeps.
My childhood summers blur together, a haze of sprinklers and sticky lollies.
I have a scar across my right palm from a kitchen knife at age eleven.
Every term I fall behind in maths, then cram the week before the exam.
Our neighbour lends me her ladder and never once asks for it back quickly.
Give me a wool jumper over any synthetic fleece, even in the middle of July.
I forgot the eggs on the stove, and the kitchen smelled like a burnt tyre for days.
I can whistle through two fingers loud enough to call the dog from three streets away.
We grew up in a farmhouse at the edge of a town with one traffic light.
My commute is forty minutes on a bus that smells faintly of wet umbrellas.
I cannot run anymore since the knee surgery, and I miss it more than I admit.
Hearing the rain on the skylight makes me feel safe, like a child under a blanket.
My job is pricing insurance claims, which means reading sad stories all day.
I still remember the exact tune from my first school play, though not my lines.
My body runs warm, so I sleep with the window cracked even in January.
I took piano lessons for a decade and still cannot read music fluently.
I married my best friend from school, which my mother still finds faintly suspicious.
My favourite books are the dog-eared paperbacks I bought for a pound each.
Last spring I sent my boss the wrong spreadsheet, and the whole team saw it.
Reading a room is my strongest skill, which is useful when my kids are plotting something.
I was the second of four siblings in a rented flat above a laundrette.
After dinner I walk the dog around the block twice, then pretend I am going to bed early.
Heights make my stomach drop, so I never climb ladders, even for the Christmas lights.
Sometimes a stranger's rudeness on the bus leaves me shaking for an hour.
Most afternoons I drive a delivery van across the moors, listening to audiobooks.
Old photographs help me, though the faces in them feel like strangers now.
My heartbeat picks up on the stairs, and my breath comes in short gasps.
Night classes after my shift taught me to type properly, mostly through sheer stubbornness.
My teenage son rolls his eyes at me constantly, then leans on my shoulder during films.
I prefer walking to the shops over driving, unless it is pouring down.
I once mocked a friend's haircut in front of her new boyfriend, and I still wince.
I can name every bird at the lake by its call, though I cannot spell most of them.
Mum still tells the story of my arrival, which happened during a thunderstorm.
I wake before the sun, make tea, and read the paper while the radiator clanks.
I get tired by mid-afternoon, and no amount of coffee fixes it.
I get a low, heavy dread on Sunday nights, and I cannot always say why.
I am a nurse on a surgical ward, and my feet hurt by the end of every shift.
I forget where I put my glasses roughly four times a day, usually on my head.
After the fall my left leg stiffens, and a metal pin sits somewhere in my hip.
My teacher made me recite the times tables until they stuck, and they did.
My ex still sends a birthday card each year, and I still keep them all.
Cold showers in the morning are my one indulgence, which nobody else understands.
A flat tyre on the motorway taught me to check the spare before every long trip.
Give me a hammer and a Saturday and I will fix the gate, badly but durably.
Somewhere in a shoebox there is a photo of me at three, covered in mud.
Most evenings I cook something simple, eat it with the telly on, and wash up badly.
My budget stops at the end of the month, whatever I wish for.
Walking into my childhood kitchen always makes my throat go tight.
I cut hair in a small salon above the chemist, and I love the gossip.
When Dad told the story of the lighthouse trip, I could almost see the gulls.
My blood pressure is high and my ankles swell by evening, so I wear compression socks.
Last winter I started learning Welsh from a phone app, one lesson at a time.
Lately my youngest treats me like a lodger who forgot the house rules.
If I had a choice, I would take a rainy seaside walk over any city break.
Snapping at my little brother over nothing is the slip I regret most, and I apologised late.
I can carry three grocery bags and a toddler up four flights without setting anything down.
I grew up in a river town where everyone knew which dog belonged to whom.
On Tuesdays I take the kids to swimming, then sit in a freezing bleacher with a flask.
I cannot keep a secret for longer than an afternoon, which my friends find exhausting.
Losing my first dog left a hole that I did not expect to feel for years.
Twice a week I haul crates of vegetables into the café kitchen before dawn.
I keep a diary in a battered notebook, because my head loses things fast.
My skin burns in July, and freckles spread across my shoulders every summer.
I failed my driving test twice before I finally learned to check my mirrors.
My best mate moved abroad last year, and our calls now happen across time zones.
I dislike loud television in the next room, and wet socks most of all.
I sometimes say yes to everything, then drown in commitments and resent them.
Mental arithmetic is one of my few gifts, though my handwriting has never been legible.
My parents met at a dance hall in the winter of a year nobody remembers exactly.
My routine is coffee, a walk to the post office, and a long nap I pretend is work.
My hearing dropped in my left ear, so I sit on the right side of every table.
Anger flares fast in me, then drains away and leaves me embarrassed.
I repair old pianos in a damp garage, shaving felt and tuning by ear.
My ex and I still argue about a holiday from twelve years ago, and neither of us remembers it.
I have flat feet and a crooked little toe that never quite lines up.
Woodworking classes taught me that patience matters more than talent with a chisel.
My husband knows exactly how I like my tea, and he never has to ask.
A hot water bottle on my feet is the only thing that gets me through January.
Last month I double-booked two weddings, and both couples were very gracious about it.
I am good with children who are scared of water, having once been one myself.
Our family moved south when I was six, after a flood took the lower field.
I shower at night because mornings in my flat are a cold, rushed scramble.
Night driving is out for me since my eyes started struggling with headlights.
There is a quiet joy in an empty train carriage at dawn, all mine for a while.
Shifts at the warehouse are long, and my back complains by Thursday.
Each morning I wake up not knowing whether the dream I had was happy.
My hands are cold most of the year, and my nails break if I forget gloves.
I picked up knitting from a neighbour on the bus, and now I cannot stop.
A nephew once apologized to me for forgetting my name, and I cried a little.
My favourite colour is mustard yellow, though I own far too little of it.
When the kids were small I shouted at them over a spilt glass of milk.
Fixing a leaky tap is easy for me; the hard part is admitting the leak was my fault.
I was raised on a diet of church suppers and my uncle's terrible jokes.
At lunch I sit on the same bench by the canal and eat a sad sandwich.
Long meetings wear me down quickly, and by four o'clock my patience is gone.
Being told I am too sensitive stings, even when I know the speaker means well.
Chasing invoices fills my week, and I make a joke of it to stay sane.
The school reunion brought back a flood of names I had long since buried.
I wear glasses with thick lenses, and without them the world is a soft smear.
Every spring I try a new recipe from my grandmother's box and usually burn it.
My friends from university still meet for a pub lunch every few months.
I love crime novels with a cosy village setting and a dull, dependable detective.
I once told my nan her favourite hymn was on the wrong Sunday, and she corrected me loudly.
My sister says I can cook for six from one lonely onion and a stale heel of bread.
My birth certificate spells my surname wrong, and I have never bothered to correct it.
Weekday mornings are a blur of cereal, missing socks, and a frantic search for keys.
I was never good at languages, and my French stays stuck at the menu level.
I feel calm when the kettle is on and the radio murmurs in the other room.
I cover the council planning desk, writing up applications nobody will read.
I wrote a letter to my younger self once, and I still have the envelope.
My lungs ache in cold air, a leftover from a childhood bout of pneumonia.
I learned to swim at forty, shivering in a council pool with a red float.
Two of my closest pals drifted away after the divorce, and I miss them.
I would rather eat plain porridge at home than a fancy brunch out.
I left the back gate open overnight, and the neighbour's cat moved in for a week.
I play the cello badly but with feeling, which my neighbors have learned to tolerate.
I come from a long line of bakers, and the flour is still in our blood.
Every night at ten my husband and I stack the dishwasher, arguing about the right order.
My back aches after an hour standing, so queues are a special kind of torment.
Grief came in waves after my father died, and some mornings it still knocks.
I sell tickets at the railway station, and most of the questions are about platforms.
Dementia took my aunt's recent years first, leaving the distant ones glowing.
My back is stiff in the mornings, and my shoulders hunch from years at a desk.
I took a first aid course at work, and now I flinch at every bandage.
Every couple of weeks my cousin and I swap recipes over a shared spreadsheet.
I prefer the window seat on trains, even when the view is only a car park.
I booked the wrong train and arrived at the coast two hours after the wedding started.
Cutting hair is a skill I picked up in a dorm bathroom, and it shows.
Born in the back room of a shop, I learned to count change before I could read.
I start the day with a crossword, a glass of water, and a long look out the window.
Singing in tune is beyond me, and I have stopped trying in public.
I cried at a television advert last week and felt silly for the rest of the day.
Each shift I sweep the same floor, and by evening it looks just as dirty.
I can still hum the lullaby my mother sang, though the words are gone.
I have a bad left hip and a good right one, and I joke about the imbalance.
Mum taught me to drive a stick shift on a farm track, shouting the whole time.
When my grandmother hugs me, she smells of rosewater and I melt a little.
Honey on toast beats jam for me, and I will argue it till the kettle boils.
I often rehearse arguments in the shower and then never have them.
I can sleep on a night train, a bus, or a kitchen floor, almost anywhere.
My mother was a nurse and my father drove a bus, and both were tired all the time.
On Sundays I wander the market, buy too many apples, and carry them home in a rucksack.
Since the diagnosis I need a nap by two, and I hate that I need it.
